component_findings.async_structured: std::async and std::future/std::promise provide asynchronous composition, but there is no structured-concurrency primitive with automatic join/cancellation in the core language/standard library (no scoped task groups until very recent library additions, and no first-class cancellation token in the base model); futures must be manually managed and cancellation is not intrinsically supported, so this is a usable-but-limited baseline, level 2.
component_findings.error_cancel_propagation: Exceptions thrown inside a std::thread that are not caught within the thread terminate the program (std::terminate) rather than propagating to the joining thread by default; std::future/std::async do propagate exceptions when retrieved via .get(), giving partial, caveat-laden propagation. This is a usable baseline with real gaps ordinary users must manage, i.e. level 2.
component_findings.parallel_execution: Since C++11 the standard library provides std::thread mapping directly to OS-level native threads with true parallel execution and no default single-threaded-runtime bottleneck, and the standard memory model (std::atomic, happens-before relations) is defined for genuine multi-core execution; workloads such as those in template/workloads can be parallelized with std::thread/std::async without any documented fundamental caveat, meriting level 4.
component_findings.race_safety: C++ has no compiler-enforced static data-race prevention; concurrent shared mutable state is permitted by default and relies entirely on programmer discipline, with data races being undefined behavior rather than a compile-time or guaranteed runtime-detected error (tools like ThreadSanitizer are external/Ecosystem, out of scope here). This matches a rudimentary/high-friction level, i.e. level 1.
component_findings.synchronization_channels: The standard library offers std::mutex, std::condition_variable, std::atomic, std::lock_guard/unique_lock and (C++20) std::latch/std::barrier/semaphore as coherent, documented low-level primitives; there is no built-in high-level channel/message-passing type in the core language, so coordination is correct and idiomatic but requires composing primitives manually, matching level 3.

metric.concurrency.limitations: Findings are based on documented C++ standard concurrency semantics (std::thread, std::atomic, std::future, memory model) rather than execution of adversarial race-detection tooling inside this sandbox, since sanitizer/tool maturity is explicitly out of scope for this intrinsic-language metric. The frozen micro programs under template/programs/cpp/micro were inspected only for representative structure, not run under a race detector.
metric.concurrency.selection_rule: Judge intrinsic concurrency/parallelism semantics and core runtime primitives. External frameworks and debugger/tool maturity are out of scope.
metric.concurrency.selection_rule_applied: Judge intrinsic concurrency/parallelism semantics and core runtime primitives. External frameworks and debugger/tool maturity are out of scope.

component_findings.abi_calling_control: Calling convention and linkage are controllable through 'extern "C"', attribute-qualified linkage specifiers, and platform ABI attributes (e.g. __cdecl/__stdcall on supported compilers); this gives explicit control for the common interoperability cases but leaves some ABI details (e.g. class layout across compilers) implementation-defined, matching a strong-but-bounded level 3.
component_findings.bidirectional_callbacks: C++ has first-class function pointers, and can pass free functions or static member functions as C-compatible callbacks, and can embed foreign code/be embedded via a coherent, long-standing function-pointer and vtable-compatible design; this is a first-class, low-friction design (level 4).
component_findings.foreign_declaration: C++ declares foreign symbols via 'extern "C"' blocks and ordinary function prototypes, as used implicitly by the toolchain-level linkage model exercised when compiling programs such as template/programs/cpp/micro/mb01.cpp with a standard C++ compiler; this is explicit and understandable but requires manual header duplication rather than automatic import, so it is strong but not fully first-class (level 3).
component_findings.ownership_lifetime_boundary: Ownership and lifetime across a foreign boundary must be expressed manually: raw pointers, manual new/delete or malloc/free pairing, and no compiler-enforced boundary-lifetime contract exist at the extern "C" boundary itself (RAII/smart pointers do not cross the C ABI). This is a usable baseline with meaningful gaps that ordinary users must manage by convention, i.e. level 2.
component_findings.type_layout_mapping: The language exposes precise control of primitive, pointer, aggregate and string boundary representations through fixed-width integer types, 'struct' layout guarantees for standard-layout/POD types, alignas/alignof, and reinterpret_cast; this is a first-class, low-friction capability (level 4), directly exercised by the micro programs under template/programs/cpp/micro which rely on precise numeric/pointer types (e.g. mb04.cpp, mb08.cpp).

metric.ffi_interoperability_design.limitations: No live compiler diagnostics or ABI-mismatch adversarial tests were executed in this sandbox; judgment relies on documented C++ language/ABI semantics and the structure of the frozen micro-benchmark programs available under template/programs/cpp/micro, not on a network-sourced standard text. Cross-compiler C++ ABI compatibility (beyond the C-compatible subset) is intrinsically implementation-defined and is reflected in the level assigned rather than treated as an external maturity concern.
metric.ffi_interoperability_design.selection_rule: Judge intrinsic FFI/ABI boundary design, not breadth of existing third-party bindings (Ecosystem).
metric.ffi_interoperability_design.selection_rule_applied: Judge intrinsic FFI/ABI boundary design, not breadth of existing third-party bindings (Ecosystem).
